items.title: From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
items.abstract_text: Debate over the role of generative artificial intelligence in formal education is marked by sharply divergent claims about its effects on student learning. Much of this disagreement reflects a failure to distinguish immediate performance gains from durable learning. This article addresses a central gap in the literature by focusing on when and how students should be permitted to rely on AI. It introduces the Gradual Release of AI-Technology (GRAIT) model, extending Pearson and Gallagher’s gradual release of responsibility to the staged use of cognitively substantive AI-technologies in formal education. The model distinguishes gradual release of responsibility, which concerns who performs the cognitive work, from gradual release of technology, which concerns when and how that work may be scaffolded, augmented, or offloaded. Three phases are proposed: independent cognition, where foundational knowledge and skill are developed without AI substitution; shared (entangled) cognition, where AI is introduced through constrained, teacher-guided interaction; and offloaded cognition, where learners strategically delegate and reallocate aspects of thinking once risks to learning are minimal and opportunities emerge elsewhere. Progression depends on demonstrated knowledge, skill proficiency, and epistemic readiness. The central question is not whether students should use AI, but who should use it, when, how, and under what conditions it should be embraced or avoided.

items.abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interconnected mechanisms underlying GenAI-mediated learning, while AI literacy and learner agency functioned as enabling conditions. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. When these functions are increasingly delegated to AI, assistance may become cognitive substitution, potentially weakening independent engagement and learner control. Productive augmentation and problematic dependence thus depend primarily on how cognitive and regulatory responsibility is organized. The Metacognition-Trust-Co-Regulation (MTC) Framework integrates these processes into a unified theoretical account. It explains how cognitive activity can be distributed between learners and AI while preserving human agency as the organizing principle of learning. AI literacy and learner agency are conceptualized not as additional MTC mechanisms but as enabling conditions that help learners understand GenAI's capabilities and limitations, calibrate reliance, and retain ownership of learning. The framework therefore provides a basis for explaining variation in psychological and learning outcomes, including autonomy, motivation, confidence, engagement, cognitive load, feedback literacy, and agency. The principal contribution of this review is to specify the psychological conditions under which GenAI becomes educationally productive, rather than characterizing it as inherently beneficial or detrimental. This perspective shifts attention from evaluating GenAI primarily as an instructional technology toward understanding how learners regulate its use while preserving the cognitive activities through which learning occurs. Future research should empirically test the MTC Framework across learner populations, language tasks, educational settings, and GenAI systems. Longitudinal, experimental, and processsensitive designs are needed to examine whether the proposed relationships among metacognition, trust, and co-regulation remain robust across contexts and over time. Research should also identify when human-AI cognitive partnerships enhance learning without displacing essential cognitive and regulatory activities. items.abstract_text: This study examines how undergraduate students integrate generative AI tools into home exams and how these practices relate to self-regulated learning (SRL) and academic performance. Using a mixed-methods design, we analyzed exam responses, self-reports, and performance data from 891 students enrolled in BA-level qualitative methodology courses (2023–2024). Students were permitted to use AI if they disclosed their usage. Three modes of AI engagement were identified: instrumental (task completion with minimal evaluation), ideational (idea generation and selective integration), and reflective (critical evaluation and feedback-driven refinement). At a general level, AI use was associated with increased efficiency and somewhat higher performance than non-use. However, these aggregate patterns masked substantial variation across modes of use. Instrumental use was associated with weaker performance in some tasks, including definition tasks where reliance on generic AI-generated responses did not align with course-specific criteria. In contrast, reflective engagement with AI was associated with stronger and more consistent performance. Interpreted through an SRL framework, these findings suggest that outcomes of AI use depend on how students regulate its use. Rather than uniformly supporting or undermining learning, AI appears to amplify differences in students’ self-regulatory capacities. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing skills for critical and reflective engagement with AI.

analysis.methods: The study was conducted in the "Introduction to Qualitative Methods" course offered to undergraduate students in the Faculty of Social Sciences at the University of Eastern Finland. The compulsory course is taken in the second or third year by students in social sciences, health and social management, business, geography, and open university. Instruction and assessment were conducted in Finnish (quotes are translated into English). The dataset is based on a home exam consisting of three tasks. The first task asked students to define a key concept in qualitative research. To receive the maximum score, students had to provide an accurate definition, elaborate on it using course materials, and contextualize it within qualitative research. The second task assessed students' ability to apply a qualitative analysis method to a short dataset. High-scoring responses included an appropriate research question, a description of the selected method, a clear account of the analytical process (coding and theme development), and a coherent interpretation of findings. The third task required students to evaluate the methodological and ethical aspects of a research setting. Full credit required identifying strengths and limitations in relation to research questions, data collection, analysis, and ethics. Emphasis was placed on internal consistency, that is, recognizing how individual design choices combine into a coherent qualitative approach. The study used authentic course data, meaning that assessment was conducted by the course instructor as part of the normal course process, and the research began only after grading had been completed. Consequently, inter-rater reliability was not calculated. However, the use of a structured rubric and the re-evaluation of a subset of responses supported consistency in grading. Students received information about the research via the course page and email, and those who declined participation were excluded. The study complied with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, 2016/679) and the Finnish Data Protection Act (1050/2018). All data were pseudonymized prior to analysis. The dataset includes home exam materials from 413 students in 2023 and 478 students in 2024 (total N = 891). We used five types of data: exam answers, platform log data, exam results, self-reported AI use, and course feedback (Table 1 ). Each dataset served a distinct role within a mixed-methods design. Exam answers, self-reports, and feedback formed the basis for qualitative analysis of AI use, while performance (points and grades) and log data (completion time) supported quantitative analysis of outcomes and efficiency. After course completion, we compiled all exam data into a spreadsheet containing exam year, submission time, task scores, total points, final grade, and self-reported AI use. Anonymous course feedback was not linked to individual students and was analyzed separately. The qualitative analysis focused on exams in which students reported AI use. We conducted a thematic analysis to identify patterns in AI use (Braun & Clarke, 2021) . The coding proceeded in four steps: 1) inductive coding of self-reports, 2) identification of recurring patterns, 3) deductive coding of exam responses with cross-validation to self-reports based on created criteria, and 4) deductive coding of course feedback. We identified three modes of AI use: instrumental, ideational, and reflective. In self-reports students described instrumental use as editing or directly adapting AI-generated text, ideational use as using AI for idea generation, and reflective use as evaluating their writing with AI tools. The first author conducted the initial inductive coding, after which the third author reviewed coding. Rather than conducting independent blind coding, the review process focused on evaluating the conceptual coherence of the categories, discussing ambiguous cases, and refining category boundaries. Particular attention was given to distinctions between instrumental and ideational use, which were less clearly differentiated than reflective use. Specifically, some students used AI primarily for improving language, grammar, or structure while leaving the substantive content largely unchanged. After discussion, these cases were classified as instrumental use because AI functioned mainly as an editing tool rather than as a source of ideas or reflective feedback. Because many self-reports were brief, we developed additional classification criteria (typical indicators) to support the following deductive coding. To refine these criteria, we compared a sample of student responses from each mode with example answers generated by ChatGPT 3.5, which was used by 85% of the students, and with established indicators of AI-generated text (Simon, 2023) . We focused on three dimensions: 1) content (superficial analysis, contextual misalignment, generic responses and factual inconsistencies in relation to course materials), 2) structure (formulaic organization, weak logical connections, mechanical use of transitions, and similar structural patterns across task types), and 3) style (overly formal tone, overly polished appearance, generic or vague wording, repetitiveness, lack of personal voice). Instrumental use was coded when AI-generated content formed the primary basis of the response with minimal modification. Ideational use was coded when AI outputs were selectively integrated into student-authored text. Reflective use was coded when AI was used primarily to refine students' own responses. In ambiguous cases, classification was based on the dominant pattern across content, structure, and style indicators. Together, we used these steps to develop the coding scheme (Appendix 1). analysis.discussion: Our findings suggest a gradual normalization of AI use in academic settings, reflected in increased uptake and more positive attitudes, aligning with prior research indicating generally neutral or positive student perceptions of AI in education (Ardelean & Edit, 2023; Jinchuña Huallpa et al., 2023) . However, ethical concerns persisted, particularly regarding whether AI-assisted exam work constitutes genuine learning. Similar student concerns have been identified in contexts AI use may compromise fairness and skill development (Chaudhry et al., 2023) . Overall, the findings challenge the notion of students as uniform adopters of AI. Instead, attitudes and emotions toward AI differ, shaping how and whether students use LLMs in academic tasks. This variation underlines the need for more nuanced, context-sensitive accounts of AI use in authentic learning situations. This study shows that students' use of AI in academic tasks is not uniform but varies in meaningful ways. We identified three modes of AI use-instrumental, ideational, and reflective-and found that these are associated with different levels of engagement and performance. Students who engaged more evaluatively with AI tended to demonstrate stronger and more consistent outcomes, while more instrumental use was sometimes associated with weaker performance, especially in tasks requiring contextualization and critical interpretation. Taken together, these findings indicate that the role of AI in learning depends on how students use it. AI is not inherently beneficial or harmful; rather, its effects depend on how students regulate its use. In this sense, AI makes students' self-regulatory capacities more visible and potentially more consequential. This highlights the importance of supporting students in developing the skills needed to use AI thoughtfully and critically, so that it contributes to meaningful learning rather than mere task completion.
analysis.limitations: This study has several limitations. First, the data were collected during the early stages of widespread generative AI adoption, when many students were still experimenting with the technology. As a result, the proposed categorization of AI use should be considered an initial framework, open to further refinement. In addition, the study was conducted in the context of home exams, which represent a specific assessment setting. Comparisons to more complex academic tasks, such as thesis writing, should therefore be made with caution, as students may employ multiple AI strategies across extended projects and use a wider range of tools. Second, the study is based on naturally occurring data without experimental control. Consequently, self-regulated learning processes were inferred rather than directly measured. The analysis relies primarily on self-reports, which varied in detail and did not include prompts, limiting insight into actual AI interactions. This may have affected the classification of AI use, particularly in distinguishing between ideational and reflective modes. In addition, it is possible that some students did not disclose their AI use, which could lead to under-or overestimation of differences between groups. As AI models evolved rapidly during data collection (2023-2024), differences in tool capabilities may have influenced the effectiveness of certain usage strategies. And variation in exam tasks across sessions may also affect comparability, despite the use of a shared grading rubric. A further limitation concerns interpretation. As an observational and mainly qualitative study, the findings indicate associations rather than causal relationships. In particular, students who engaged in more evaluative or reflective forms of AI use may already have differed from others in terms of prior ability, motivation, or self-regulatory capacity. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether differences in performance are related to AI use itself or to underlying student characteristics. The study is also limited by its theoretical framing. Although selfregulated learning provided a useful framework for identifying differences in students' AI use, the aim was not to measure or validate SRL processes as such. Consequently, the findings primarily, and somewhat simplistically, draw attention to students' self-regulation in integrating AI as a learning resource. Alternative theoretical perspectives, such as deep learning or digital literacy, might have provided greater insight into the learning processes themselves or the critical skills required to use AI tools. Both of these aspects deserve further exploration. Thus, the study provides only partial access to students' learning processes. While self-reports and feedback offer useful insights, they do not capture students' internal motivations, planning strategies, or realtime decision-making. In particular, motivational factors such as task value, goal orientation, and self-efficacy were not directly measured, even though the findings suggest they play an important role in shaping AI use. Given the complexity of motivation as a research domain, future studies would benefit from employing methods specifically designed to capture these dimensions more systematically. The findings cannot be generalized statistically to all higher education contexts where students use generative AI for written assignments. The study is based on an authentic teaching situation, with all its inherent imperfections, and it began as a qualitative and conceptual process to which quantitative elements were added later on. The findings should therefore be interpreted as indicative rather than definitive. However, the consistency of the identified patterns across two academic years suggests that the distinction between instrumental, ideational, and reflective AI use may have relevance beyond the specific course examined here. Despite these limitations, the study highlights the complex and nonuniform role of AI in educational settings. Drawing on authentic assessment context, longitudinal design spanning two academic years, and triangulated data, the study provides a robust account of how students engage with AI in practice. The findings suggest that the pedagogical value of AI depends less on the tool itself and more on how students regulate its use within learning processes. The findings may inform educational decision-making in several ways. First, they suggest that educational interventions should focus not only on whether students use AI, but also on how they use it. Second, instruction on AI literacy should emphasize critical evaluation, adaptation, and reflection rather than task completion. Third, assessment practices may benefit from rewarding contextualization, critical thinking, and reflective engagement, which appear to distinguish higher-performing forms of AI use. Future research should examine how instructional approaches and targeted support can help students engage with AI in ways that sustain autonomy, critical thinking, and deep learning.

items.abstract_text:
Introduction 
                     The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has generated increasing concern regarding its influence on students' epistemic agency, critical thinking, and cognitive autonomy. This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on the epistemic implications of GenAI in higher education, with particular emphasis on the tension between cognitive offloading and critical autonomy. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 were identified through systematic searches in Scopus, the Web of Science Core Collection, and seven education and multidisciplinary databases accessed through EBSCOhost. Eligible studies examined the educational use of generative AI systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and similar large language models within higher education contexts. Data extraction and thematic synthesis were conducted to identify recurring epistemic, cognitive, pedagogical, and ethical patterns across the included studies. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     The findings reveal that GenAI simultaneously functions as a cognitive scaffold and a source of epistemic vulnerability. While AI-assisted learning environments may support feedback literacy, metacognitive reflection, conceptual clarification, and self-regulated learning, uncritical reliance on AI-generated outputs was frequently associated across the included studies with cognitive offloading, automation bias, superficial information processing, diminished analytical engagement, and weakened evaluative judgment. The evidence further suggests that the educational consequences of GenAI are mediated primarily by pedagogical design, AI literacy, and assessment practices rather than by the technology itself. 
                   
                   
                     Discussion 
                     Overall, the review supports the need for higher education institutions to promote critical AI literacy and pedagogical frameworks capable of preserving epistemic agency, reflective reasoning, and cognitive autonomy in increasingly AI-mediated learning environments.

When findings extended the scope of the original framework, the domain was refined through the addition of new interpretive components. items.abstract_text: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has altered how students access information, complete academic tasks, and participate in learning activities. Alongside these opportunities, GenAI introduces technology-related demands that may be associated with students' learning engagement. This study examined the relationship between generative AI technostress and learning engagement, with academic adaptability examined as a statistical mediator and AI literacy as a moderator of this relationship. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was adopted. Using nonprobability convenience sampling, data were collected through an online self-report questionnaire administered via Wenjuanxing to undergraduate students with experience using GenAI for academic purposes at Northeast Normal University in China. A total of 529 valid responses were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrap-based conditional process analysis. Generative AI technostress was negatively associated with academic adaptability and learning engagement, whereas academic adaptability was positively associated with learning engagement. A significant indirect association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement through academic adaptability was identified, while the direct association remained significant. AI literacy also moderated the negative association between generative AI technostress and academic adaptability, with a weaker negative association observed among students reporting higher AI literacy. The conditional indirect association through academic adaptability was stronger at lower levels of AI literacy. Taken together, the findings indicate that the relationship between generative AI technostress and learning engagement is associated with students' capacity to adapt to changing academic demands and varies according to their level of AI literacy.

The target population consisted of undergraduate students with experience using generative AI tools for academic purposes. The accessible population comprised undergraduate students enrolled at Northeast Normal University during the data collection period. Northeast Normal University was selected as the data collection site because the author was engaged in a collaborative research exchange at the university during the study period, which provided direct access to the student population and facilitated field data collection. A nonprobability convenience sampling strategy was used. Eligible undergraduate students were invited to participate through their academic counselors. The counselors distributed a Wenjuanxing survey link or QR code to students through student communication groups. Participation was voluntary, and students completed the online questionnaire independently using their own electronic devices. Data were collected between March 1, 2026 and July 1, 2026 using Wenjuanxing, a widely used online survey platform in China. It also accords with recent work suggesting that difficulty managing AI-related demands may be associated with lower involvement in learning activities. However, Lallmahomed (2025) reported a more differentiated pattern among university students in Mauritius, finding that hindrance techno-stressors were negatively associated with student engagement, whereas challenge techno-stressors were positively associated with engagement. The mediation result suggests that part of the association between GenAI technostress and engagement is related to students’ capacity to adjust their cognition, behavior, and emotions when learning conditions change. Academic adaptability therefore provides a plausible psychological explanation for why students reporting greater GenAI-related stress also tend to report lower engagement. Given the cross-sectional design, however, this finding should be interpreted as an indirect association rather than a causal process. AI literacy moderated the negative association between generative AI technostress and academic adaptability, with a weaker negative association among students reporting higher AI literacy. This pattern is consistent with research suggesting that stronger AI-related knowledge and competence are associated with greater ability to understand AI functions, evaluate outputs, and manage AI-supported learning activities ( Ng et al., 2021 ; Bećirović et al., 2025 ; Bewersdorff et al., 2025 ). Students with greater AI literacy may have clearer expectations about AI capabilities and limitations and may therefore experience less uncertainty when deciding how to use AI in academic work. The moderated mediation analysis further showed that the negative indirect association between generative AI technostress and learning engagement through academic adaptability was stronger at lower levels of AI literacy and weaker at higher levels. This suggests that the relationship between technostress and engagement varies according to both students’ adaptive capacity and their AI-related competence. Rather than operating independently, academic adaptability and AI literacy appear to represent complementary elements of students’ adjustment to GenAI-mediated learning. The findings provide several implications for the application of the transactional theory of stress and coping to GenAI-mediated learning. The negative associations of generative AI technostress with academic adaptability and learning engagement support the theory’s proposition that individuals’ responses to environmental demands depend on appraisal and adjustment processes rather than on the objective presence of the demand alone ( Folkman, 2013 ). More importantly, the mediation finding extends this perspective by identifying academic adaptability as a specific adjustment-related construct through which perceived AI-related demands are associated with learning engagement. The findings therefore help distinguish between the experience of technological demands and students’ capacity to adjust to those demands in AI-mediated learning environments. The results also refine the application of conservation of resources theory. AI literacy has generally been conceptualized as knowledge, practical competence, evaluation, and ethical understanding ( Long and Magerko, 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ). This extends COR theory to AI-mediated higher education by indicating that the protective value of a resource may depend partly on its relevance to the specific demands being encountered. Taken together, the findings provide an integrated theoretical account of the proposed model. The transactional theory of stress and coping explains the technostress–adaptability–engagement pathway, whereas conservation of resources theory helps explain why the technostress–adaptability association varies according to AI literacy. The moderated mediation result supports this combined interpretation by showing that the indirect association through adaptability differs across levels of the proposed personal resource. Introduction 
                     Writing with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve a supported product without necessarily strengthening the competence that remains after support is removed. This study examined that distinction through a layer-sensitive account of cognitive offloading. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     In this eight-week quasi-experimental classroom study, 180 Chinese undergraduates from six intact English academic-writing classes entered the study and 168 completed the protocol. Two classes were assigned to each of three conditions: no-AI writing, bounded AI support with compulsory reflection, and open AI collaboration. Students completed a baseline task, three intervention assignments, and a supervised Week 8 independent no-AI near-transfer task. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     
                      Open AI collaboration had the highest observed supported-writing mean (
                       M 
                      = 4.02), although the class-clustered open–bounded contrast was imprecise (adjusted difference = 0.21, 95% CI [0.06, 0.36], wild-cluster
                       p 
                      = 0.064). At Week 8, the bounded-support condition showed higher adjusted outcomes than open collaboration in writing quality (difference = 0.27), higher-order thinking (0.35), argument depth (0.42), and independent revision quality (0.39); exact wild-cluster
                       p 
                      values ranged from 0.050 to 0.063. Within the 112 AI-exposed students, open collaboration involved more prompts, greater text incorporation, less self-generated text, and deeper idea and reasoning offloading. An adjusted associative decomposition showed that open collaboration predicted higher aggregate offloading (
                       a 
                      = 0.77,
                       SE 
                      = 0.06), which was associated with lower Week 8 higher-order thinking (
                       b 
                      = −0.45,
                       SE 
                      = 0.08); the bootstrap indirect estimate was −0.34, 95% CI [−0.48, −0.21]. Self-regulated writing attenuated, but did not eliminate, this negative association.
                     
                   
                   
                     Discussion 
                     Because conditions were allocated by only six intact classes and the bounded condition combined delegation restrictions with compulsory reflection, the results are interpreted as classroom-level, mechanism-consistent associations rather than definitive causal effects. The findings distinguish performance achieved with GenAI from competence demonstrated independently after support is removed.

items.abstract_text: Generative AI tools are increasingly embedded in everyday work and learning, yet their fluency, opacity, and propensity to hallucinate mean that users must critically evaluate AI outputs rather than accept them at face value. The present research conceptualises critical thinking in AI use as a dispositional tendency to verify the source and content of AI-generated information, to understand how models work and where they fail, and to reflect on the broader implications of relying on AI. Across six studies ( N = 1341), we developed and validated the 13-item critical thinking in AI use scale and mapped its nomological network. Study 1 generated and content-validated scale items. Study 2 supported a three-factor structure (Verification, Motivation, and Reflection). Studies 3 and 4 confirmed the higher-order model, demonstrated strong factor loadings, internal consistency, sex invariance, convergent and discriminant evidence for validity, and showed that critical thinking in AI use was positively associated with openness, extraversion, positive trait affect, and frequency of AI use. Study 5 supported the scale's test-retest reliability. Lastly, Study 6 demonstrated criterion evidence of validity for the scale, with higher critical thinking in AI use scores predicting more frequent and diverse verification strategies, greater veracity judgement accuracy in a novel and naturalistic GPT-powered AI chatbot fact-checking task, and deeper reflection about responsible AI. The current work clarifies why and how people exercise oversight over generative AI outputs and provides a validated scale and ecologically grounded paradigm to support theory testing, cross-group, and longitudinal research on critical thinking in AI use.

Taken together, these findings position the critical thinking in AI use scale as a reliable and valid tool for advancing research on critical thinking in the context of using generative AI tools, clarifying its correlates, and informing interventions to support more responsible AI use. In conclusion, this work provides a comprehensive first account of critical thinking in AI use as a measurable construct that captures stable individual differences and has realworld benefits for how people engage with generative AI. Across six studies, we introduced a theoretically grounded and empirically validated instrument that captures how users verify the source and content of AI outputs, seek to understand model behaviour and limits, and reflect responsibly on personal, social, and ethical implications of AI use. The critical thinking in AI use scale exhibited a clear three-factor structure with a higher-order factor, strong internal consistency, temporal stability, convergent and discriminant validity, and measurement invariance across sex. Critical thinking in AI use was systematically patterned by frequency of AI use, positive affect, and personality traits such as openness and extraversion. Importantly, critical thinking in AI use generalises beyond self-report, providing evidence about what AI users actually do, not just what they intend. Higher critical thinking in AI use predicts more frequent and diverse verification methods, better veracity-judgement accuracy in a generative-AI fact-checking task, and deeper reflection in a reflective writing task. Critical thinking in AI use supports calibrated, responsible AI use by encouraging engagement with AI while maintaining human oversight of its outputs. analysis.limitations: While the present research provides a foundational understanding of critical thinking in AI use, it has a few limitations that should be acknowledged and that open avenues for future research. First, our data fully relies on English-speaking online and university samples. Competencies that relate to critical thinking in AI use, such as AI literacy (Chung & Wihbey, 2024; Mansoor et al., 2024) and misinformation susceptibility (M. Chan et al., 2025; Kyrychenko et al., 2025; Maertens et al., 2024; Roozenbeek et al., 2020) have demonstrated cross-cultural variations. Future work should test critical thinking in AI use across cultures, languages, and organisational settings, examining measurement invariance and group differences to strengthen the generalisability of the scale. Second, the present studies did not include direct measures of (generative) AI literacy. As a result, we were unable to examine how critical thinking in AI use relates to people's declarative and procedural knowledge about AI systems, or whether the scale predicts outcomes over and above AI literacy. Given frameworks that conceptualise AI literacy as a prerequisite for competent and responsible AI use (Long & Magerko, 2020; Mills et al., 2024) , future research should include validated AI literacy measures to test their overlap, discriminant validity, and incremental predictive value for verification behaviour and real-world AI outcomes. Lastly, we did not assess participants' prior knowledge or expertise in the substantive domains of the veracity-judgement tasks. Domain knowledge may shape how individuals evaluate AI outputs, and it may interact with AI outputs (Dikmen & Burns, 2022) , for example, by enabling high-critical thinking in AI use individuals to detect subtle inaccuracies in AI-generated content. Future studies should therefore measure and experimentally manipulate topic knowledge to clarify how critical thinking in AI use combines with domain-specific expertise in guiding verification behaviour.
